note: Zone separability -- can a floorplan hold two temperatures at once? Built 29 Aug 2026 against Sections 1.14 and 10.8 of Photonic_Cooling_Devices___v9.pdf, which propose a die with hot dynamic-dominated compute islands beside cold static-dominated SRAM. Whether that is possible is a FLOORPLAN question and this is the measurement of it.
why_a_new_metric: Every prior floorplan metric here answered 'how hard is this die to cool', with cooling meaning pull the peak down. relative_plateau was the last standing and it failed its transfer test on 28 Aug. The architecture reframing needs a different question entirely, so the vacancy and the new requirement arrived together.

MEASURED_the_premise_checks_out_and_more.source: McPAT block_powers_split on the project trace (linpack, 7nm, T_ref 330 K)
MEASURED_the_premise_checks_out_and_more.verdict: 34.6% measured, so the premise holds. The sharper point the book does not make: 89% of ALL leakage on this die is in L3 alone, and L2-within-core is 80.3% static against 0.3% for the FPU. The cold zone is not a partition anyone has to impose -- it is already where the leakage lives, in one contiguous structure.

THE_PHYSICS_die_thickness_cancels.result: G_monolithic = k_Si * boundary_length, INDEPENDENT of die thickness
THE_PHYSICS_die_thickness_cancels.why: across a boundary of length P in a slab of thickness t, Q = k*(P*t)*dT/L, and in a monolithic die the healing length L is not free -- a step in boundary condition heals over a distance of order t. So t cancels. Thinning shrinks the conducting cross-section and the healing length in equal measure and does not help.

and_silicon_gets_worse_as_it_cools.note: umklapp scattering freezes out, so the colder the zone the better its surroundings conduct into it

leakage_saving.note: the calibrated curve stops at 310 K and clamps below it, so 110 K of the requested cooling is unevidenced -- see Section 10.8 vs leakage_calibration/

MEASURED_neither_floorplan_can_hold_the_.verdict: 3039x and 6322x more boundary conductance than the power balance allows. And the 34-core die is WORSE than the single core, because the tiler interleaves L3 with the cores and boundary length is the whole story -- 122 mm of it. Cache laid out for latency is cache laid out for maximum zone boundary.

THE_SPEC_the_useful_output.form: max boundary conductance [W/K] = leakage saving [W] / gradient [K]
THE_SPEC_the_useful_output.why: independent of how the isolation is built -- it is what a packaging engineer needs. The floorplan sets the numerator's boundary length; the power balance sets the limit.

monolithic_vs_package.conclusion: disaggregation is NECESSARY and NOT SUFFICIENT. The cold zone has to be a physically separate die AND the package needs a deliberate thermal break. That is a packaging programme, not a floorplan optimisation.

THE_LIMIT_that_bounds_all_of_this.what: McPAT rejects temperatures outside 300-400 K outright
THE_LIMIT_that_bounds_all_of_this.consequence: our calibrated leakage curve stops at 310 K and CLAMPS below it, so every saving quoted here for a 200 K cold zone is evaluated at 310 K. 110 K of the requested cooling is unevidenced, and leakage_saving_W flags it rather than returning a bare number.
THE_LIMIT_that_bounds_all_of_this.why_it_matters: Section 10.8 claims 100-200x leakage reduction for 350->200 K. Our curve's local doubling constant is already 274 K at 310 K -- essentially flat -- which would give ~2x. Whether the flattening is a real gate/BTBT floor arriving early or a McPAT artefact decides the cold-zone prize by ~50x, and it is the highest-value open question in the architecture argument.
THE_LIMIT_that_bounds_all_of_this.how_to_close_it: PTM SPICE cards (ptm.asu.edu, free, 7nm) give leakage vs T over any range
